clues.title: Plate: white, yellow, or 'parrot' yellow left part
text: [Standard](https://maps.app.goo.gl/y3Ke88cHDERNzsJV8) plates are long and **white**, with a blue strip on the left. [Commercial](https://maps.app.goo.gl/qU3xVHvq6aXEbTdSA) plates are **yellow**. And so-called “[Parrot](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Wd1QcR8HbxzcrTGX9)” plates have a **yellow section** on the left hand side. These are unique to Denmark.
NOTE: The Netherlands, Luxembourg and the UK use yellow plates for private vehicles.

images.caption: Danish plates: standard, yellow commercial and 'parrot' yellow left part

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Standard plates are long, white with a blue strip. Commercial plates are yellow. 'Parrot' plates have a yellow section on the left and are unique here.

differs.how: Dutch private cars use fully yellow plates
Luxembourg private cars use fully yellow plates
UK private cars use yellow rear plates

clues.title: Landscape: flat, open fields between towns
text: Denmark is a generally [flat](https://goo.gl/maps/wt6BuwquwRoUX68m6) country with wide, [open fields](https://goo.gl/maps/Jb3jz3sdcsSrYGQc9) between towns. [Suburban areas](https://goo.gl/maps/17bXd4RSqqJSu26MA) are usually open, with space between buildings. Urban cores are more dense and built up.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A flat country with wide open fields between towns. Suburbs are open with space between buildings, and town centres are denser.

clues.title: Road lines: all white, double centre lines
text: Denmark has all-white road lines. **Double middle lines** are very common.
NOTE: Some other European countries, most notably Poland and Greece, can have double middle lines.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: All road lines are white, and double centre lines are very common. Poland and Greece can have double lines too.

differs.how: can also have double centre lines
can also have double centre lines

clues.title: Road lines: edge line of small white squares
text: Outer road lines often consist of **small white squares**. These unique-looking lines are a good way to identify Denmark.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Outer lines often look like a row of small white squares. A very good clue for the country.

clues.title: Sign: low direction sign in a pipe frame
text: Denmark has very unique-looking direction signs that are very useful to recognize the country. They are low to the ground and **framed by pipes**. They are either coloured [red and white](https://goo.gl/maps/xt2jxMHjMQivxS8B7) or [blue and white](https://goo.gl/maps/zC5mi95DGrvhHD8W6), with a directional arrow incorporated into the background. Signs often feature road numbers.

Some larger road signs have a more [standard layout](https://goo.gl/maps/oXjRzsLL2PQBcJC89) without the pipe frame. Highway signs have [blue or green](https://goo.gl/maps/SZ3AQjYCNbzxErT68) backgrounds.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Low, red and white or blue and white direction signs framed by pipes, with the arrow built into the background. Bigger signs have a normal layout, and highway signs are blue or green.

clues.title: Street sign: blue with white text, ends in 'vej'
text: Most Danish street names end in **“vej.”** This is the Danish word for “street.” Street signs most commonly have a blue background with white text.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most street names end in 'vej', the word for street. Street signs are mostly blue with white text.

clues.title: Bollard: white, yellow reflector, orange stripe
text: Denmark has a very recognizable white bollard with a yellow reflector and a **dark orange stripe**. This bollard is unique to the country. You may also find this [green variant](https://maps.app.goo.gl/9N1oFxNmpXjCDc5G8).
NOTE: Belgium has bollards that may look somewhat similar. However, it will never feature the orange stripe.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: White bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe, found nowhere else. A green version also exists.

differs.how: Belgian bollards look similar but never have the orange stripe

clues.title: Language: Æ, Ø and Å letters
text: **Danish** is a North Germanic language that is closely related to Swedish and Norwegian. The Danish alphabet contains these special letters: **Æ**, **Ø**, and **Å**.
NOTE: The special letters found in Danish can also be found in some of the other Northern Germanic languages:
- Norwegian uses Æ, Ø, and Å.
- Faroese uses Æ and Ø but not Å.
- Icelandic only uses Æ.
- Swedish only uses Å. In addition, Swedish uses Ä and Ö, which are not found in Danish.

images.caption: Danish text with the letters Æ Ø Å shown large

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A Scandinavian language using Æ, Ø and Å. Norwegian uses all three, Faroese has Æ and Ø, Icelandic only Æ, and Swedish Å plus Ä and Ö, which Danish lacks.

clues.title: Houses: red brick with orange, brown or black tiles
text: Much of the architecture in Denmark consists of **red brick**. Roofs often have orange, dark brown or black tiles.
NOTE: Similar brick architecture is also common in the Netherlands and Belgium.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A lot of red brick buildings with orange, dark brown or black tiled roofs. The Netherlands and Belgium look similar.

clues.title: Roofs: thatched, or grey corrugated
text: Some houses in Denmark have [**thatched roofs**](https://goo.gl/maps/aDB7vcs9VXEMNan37), especially in rural areas.
You can also sometimes find grey [**corrugated roofs**](https://goo.gl/maps/nGYSiVBbLtqLsbro8). These look somewhat similar to roofs commonly found in Baltic countries.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some houses, especially rural ones, have thatched roofs. Grey corrugated roofs also appear and look a bit like ones in the Baltic countries.

clues.title: Houses: timber frame walls
text: Some older or rural buildings have **timber frame** walls.
NOTE: Timber framing can be found in other Western and Central European countries as well, but are an especially common wall type for historical buildings in Denmark.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some older or rural buildings have timber-frame walls. Common across western and central Europe, but especially for historic buildings here.

clues.title: Sign: pipe frame bent around the sign
text: This signpost, where the pipe frame is **bent around the sign**, is unique to Denmark.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A signpost where the pipe frame is bent around the sign. Unique to this country.

clues.title: Guardrail: square B-type, no reflectors
text: Denmark has **square (normal B-type) guardrails**, with no reflectors.
NOTE: Denmark is one of only a very few European countries with this type of guardrail. For a good overview of European guardrails, see [this infographic](/images/denmark/europeguardrail.png).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Square (normal B-type) guardrails with no reflectors. Very few European countries use this type.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian sign with 5 stripes
text: This Danish pedestrian sign has **5 stripes. **Uniquely, the first and fifth stripe touch the edge of the white triangle.
NOTE: Sweden’s pedestrian sign has 4 stripes. Norway almost always has 4 stripes too, but very rarely you can find signs with 5 stripes.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The pedestrian sign has 5 stripes, with the first and fifth touching the edge of the white triangle. Sweden has 4 stripes, and Norway almost always 4.

clues.title: Sign: town entry sign, red slash when leaving
text: This unique sign is found when entering a town. When leaving, there will be a red slash through the sign.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A distinctive sign when entering a town. On the way out the same sign has a red slash through it.

clues.title: Sign: black and yellow bus stop
text: Bus stop signs in Denmark are **black and yellow**. A small sign is attached to the top of the pole, with the bus schedule underneath. Additionally, you may see this older [**blue and white**](https://goo.gl/maps/fRjTDJetFmcvkqtt6)** **version.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bus stop signs are black and yellow, with a small sign on top of the pole and the timetable below. An older blue and white version exists too.

clues.title: Chevron: red and white, low to the ground
text: This **red-and-white** chevron is found in Denmark. They are often low to the ground.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Red and white chevron signs, often set low to the ground.

clues.title: Pole: ordinary street poles are rare
text: Standard street level **utility poles are rare** in Denmark. Most of the electricity infrastructure you will find in the countryside are large, towering [overhead power lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_power_line), often near highways.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Normal roadside utility poles are rare. Most power infrastructure is large towering pylons, often near highways.

clues.title: Roadside: bicycle paths
text: You may sometimes see **bicycle paths** on the side of the road.
NOTE: Bicycle paths are also commonly seen in the Netherlands and Belgium.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bicycle paths sometimes run beside the road. Common in the Netherlands and Belgium too.

clues.title: Post box: national postal company
text: The PostNord, or Post Danmark company, is the national provider of postal services in Denmark. It uses these unique **postal boxes**.

images.caption: A red Danish post box on a brick wall; the arrow points to the PostNord logo

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The national postal company, PostNord (Post Danmark), uses distinctive post boxes.

clues.title: Gas stations: four brands shared with neighbours
text: These four **gas station brands** are common to Denmark, but each are shared between one other country:
- [**Ingo**](https://goo.gl/maps/gzK5cAGTik4myC2t6) can be found in Denmark and Sweden.
- [**Ok**](https://goo.gl/maps/ZnQyP9LSGm32coji9) can be found in Denmark and the Netherlands.
- [**Uno-X**](https://goo.gl/maps/N7BtoCnkt2mgQe5HA) and [**Yx**](https://goo.gl/maps/MnuSF8c2GA8ujdW19) can be found in Denmark and Norway.

images.caption: Four gas stations in a grid showing brands shared with neighbouring countries

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Ingo is also in Sweden, OK in the Netherlands, and Uno-X and Yx in Norway.

clues.title: Bollard: stone, red top, near cycle paths
text: You will rarely see these **stone bollards**, which may be painted red at the top, near bicycle paths.

images.caption: Small stone bollards with red tops beside a path; the red circle highlights one at top left

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Rare stone bollards, sometimes painted red on top, found near bicycle paths.

clues.title: Road numbers: ordered east to west
text: Denmark has an easy to learn **road numbering** system. They order their roads from east to west.
Roads starting with the numbers 2 to 5 are grouped by region.
Roads starting with the number 1 can be found nationwide, but the second digit still follows a rough regional distribution. Notably, Bornholm only has roads starting with the number 1.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Roads are numbered from east to west. Numbers starting 2 to 5 group by region. Roads starting with 1 are nationwide, but the second digit still follows a rough region, and Bornholm only has roads starting with 1.

clues.title: Roads: ring roads O1 to O4
text: **Ring roads** are special highways near bigger cities, labelled from O1 up to O4. The number increases from the centre, and each fully or partially encircles the city.
These cities have ring roads: Copenhagen, Odense, Aarhus, Aalborg, Hillerød, Kolding, and Velje.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Special highways around bigger cities are labelled O1 to O4, with the number going up away from the centre. Cities with them: Copenhagen, Odense, Aarhus, Aalborg, Hillerød, Kolding, Vejle.

clues.title: Bus: company by region, colour scheme
text: There are six regions in Denmark that each use a different **bus transportation company**. Each bus will have the brand written on the front, and have a unique colour scheme.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Six regions each have their own bus company, with its name on the front and its own colours.

clues.title: Sign: bus stop sign by region
text: In addition, these regions each have their own **bus stop sign**.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Each of those regions also has its own bus stop sign design.

clues.title: Roofs: thick seaweed thatch
text: These traditional “seaweed roofs” are found on the island of Læsø. They are made from a type of seaweed known as [eelgrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zostera).

clues.summary: The small island of Anholt only has older Gen 2 coverage, with grey overcast weather and a lot of sandy dirt beside the road.

clues.title: Sign: relaxed walking figure, rounded edges
text: Denmark's guy has a **chill walking posture** and has **rounded edges** on the person. Often found on **thicker, 3D blue squares**. His arms are also pointed down, unlike some similar signs found in Scandinavia.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The pedestrian figure walks in a relaxed way, with rounded edges and arms pointing down, often on a thick 3D blue square. Similar Scandinavian signs have different arms.

clues.title: Landscape: long fjords, steep green mountains
text: The landscape of the Faroe islands is characterised by long, wide fjords with jagged green mountains that rise straight out of the water, with rocky ridge lines along the mountainsides. The mountains generally look more imposing and greener than coastal mountains in Iceland, which can often be used to tell them apart.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Long wide fjords with jagged green mountains rising straight from the water and rocky ridges. They look more imposing and greener than Iceland's coastal mountains.

differs.how: Icelandic coastal mountains are less green and less imposing
